The honest catches: no confirmed public API for custom integration work, the free/Core action allowances are modest for a real book of accounts, and at two years old it carries far less production history than the CRMs it plugs into. Pick Rox if continuous account intelligence and CRM hygiene are the bottleneck; skip it if you specifically need outbound-sequence automation or a documented API.

listings.name: Salesforce Agentforce
listings.tagline: Salesforce's enterprise agentic-AI platform (rebranded "Agentforce 360") — prebuilt Service, SDR, Sales Coach and Commerce agents plus a low-code builder, running on live CRM data.
listings.verdict: Agentforce is the CRM-native heavyweight of this category — no other general-purpose platform here puts agents this close to a company's actual sales, service and commerce data, and it backs that up with genuine model-agnostic support (GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini) and a real developer surface (Agent API, Python SDK, CLI) rather than a walled-garden chatbot. The honest cost is Salesforce's own complexity: a Flex Credits/Conversations pricing model that has already reshaped itself multiple times since its October 2024 launch, a hard dependency on Data Cloud (now Data 360) for full cross-system context, and independent reports of multi-month rollouts and a real learning curve. Pick Agentforce if you're already deep in the Salesforce ecosystem and want agents acting directly on live CRM data; skip it if you want a lightweight platform you can stand up quickly outside that ecosystem, or predictable flat per-seat pricing.

listings.name: Sierra
listings.tagline: Bret Taylor’s enterprise agent platform, branded AI agents that resolve customer issues end to end, priced on outcomes.
listings.verdict: Sierra is the enterprise standard-bearer for customer-experience agents, and the pedigree is real: co-founded by Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, it reached $150M+ ARR by February 2026, has raised roughly $1.585 billion at a valuation above $15 billion, and is used across more than 40% of the Fortune 50. What sets it apart is depth, agents don’t just answer, they act, completing refunds and account changes across chat, voice, email and more, wrapped in serious tooling for building, supervising and testing them. Its outcome-based pricing (pay for resolutions, escalations free) is a genuinely aligned model. The flip side is access: it is sales-led with no public pricing, no free tier and a gated SDK, so it is neither quick to trial nor a fit for smaller teams. Pick Sierra if you are an enterprise that wants autonomous agents doing real work; skip it if you need self-serve, transparent pricing or an open API.

listings.name: SkipCalls
listings.tagline: AI phone receptionist that answers missed calls, filters spam, and books appointments for small businesses
listings.verdict: SkipCalls is a straightforward AI receptionist aimed at small businesses that lose leads to missed calls, with easy carrier-forwarding setup, spam filtering, bilingual answering, and solid integration coverage for calendars and CRMs. The main things to check before committing are the mismatched pricing between its website and app store listing and the unpublished cost of higher tiers needed for webhooks or unlimited agents.

listings.name: Synthflow AI
listings.tagline: A no-code voice AI platform for enterprise phone agents — a visual Flow Designer and a structured Build-Evaluate-Launch-Learn deployment cycle, billed by the minute in separate components.
listings.verdict: Synthflow AI's real differentiation is who can operate it: a genuinely visual, no-code Flow Designer and a named BELL deployment methodology mean an operations or CX team can design, test and launch a phone agent without an engineering ticket — a different buyer than the developer-first Vapi and Retell AI. That is backed by real scale ($20M Series A led by Accel, 45M+ calls processed) and an unusually complete compliance set (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, ISO 27001) for the funding stage. The honest catches are the same component-pricing pattern its rivals share — the $0.09/min headline is one of three billed pieces, and a real configuration lands near $0.11–$0.16/min before add-ons — plus no self-serve monthly plan (only metered usage or a ~$30,000/year Enterprise contract) and an LLM choice currently limited to OpenAI models. Pick Synthflow if you want a no-code path to a compliant phone agent and don't need to choose your own model; skip it if you want full API control, any-LLM flexibility, or a predictable low-commitment self-serve price.

listings.name: Undermind
listings.tagline: An AI literature-discovery agent that reads hundreds of full papers and follows citation trails, then reports how much of the literature it actually covered.
listings.verdict: Undermind is the discovery-focused entry in this category: instead of screening papers you already found against inclusion criteria (Elicit's job) or answering an open-web question (Perplexity, Manus, GC AI's different domains), it tries to find the papers a conventional keyword search misses, by reading full texts and following citation trails, and it tells you roughly how complete that search was via its "discovery curve" model. An independent peer-reviewed review backs the core pitch — it genuinely surfaces papers others miss — but the same review is equally direct about the trade-offs: no reproducible search strategy (its self-described "Achilles heel"), an 8-10 minute turnaround too slow for point-of-care use, and no MeSH integration. It also has no API today, unlike Elicit. Pick Undermind when the job is exploratory discovery or a novelty check on a niche or cross-disciplinary question; pick Elicit instead when you need a documented, repeatable screening process for a formal systematic review.

listings.name: Unify
listings.tagline: A single conversational GTM agent for warm outbound — self-serve from $0, built to augment a seller rather than replace one.
listings.verdict: Unify fills a real, previously under-served position in this category's GTM-outbound cluster: cheaper and far more transparent than Clay's usage-based ($167+/month) enrichment canvas, and self-serve where 11x and Artisan are both entirely custom-quoted and sales-gated. It explicitly positions itself as a productivity layer for a human seller rather than an autonomous replacement, wrapping list-building, enrichment, signal-based prioritization and sequencing into one chat-based agent instead of a spreadsheet-style workflow builder. The catch: it just completed a dramatic pricing-model pivot — several third-party sources published within the last few months still describe a completely different enterprise-only motion — so treat pricing found outside unifygtm.com/pricing itself as potentially stale, and its deepest features (GPT-5.5, write-access CRM sync, website intent signals) still sit behind a custom Business tier. Pick Unify if you want an accessible, self-serve GTM agent that augments a rep rather than replacing one; skip it if you specifically want Clay's build-your-own depth or 11x/Artisan's fully autonomous outbound motion.

listings.name: Vapi
listings.tagline: The developer platform for voice AI agents, bring your own model, voice and telephony, and Vapi orchestrates the call.
listings.verdict: Vapi is the builder’s choice for voice AI: an API-first, model-agnostic platform that hands developers control over every layer — transcription, model, voice and telephony — with real-time orchestration and sub-500ms latency. Its bring-your-own-provider design means you can chase the best model or cheapest voice without rebuilding the agent, and enterprise features (HIPAA, zero-data-retention, SLAs) let it scale to millions of calls. The honest catch is cost transparency: the $0.05/min headline is only the orchestration fee, and the true all-in rate is usually several times that once you add a model, a good voice and telephony. Pick Vapi if you have engineers who want to build a bespoke voice agent and own the stack; skip it if you want a no-code tool that hides the plumbing.

listings.name: Vecbase
listings.tagline: A shared workspace where AI agents with roles like Researcher, Coder, and Writer work as a team
listings.verdict: Vecbase packages multi-agent collaboration, shared memory and files, built-in AI capabilities, and one-click integrations into a single subscription, which is appealing for teams tired of stitching together separate tools. The tradeoffs are a hard cap of 10 agents per workspace, usage-based overage billing on top of the base plan, no free trial, and documentation that leans heavily on Chinese, all worth weighing before committing.

listings.name: Warmly
listings.tagline: Website-visitor de-anonymization plus two named AI agents — Inbound Agent and TAM Agent — that engage and route identified visitors automatically.
listings.verdict: Warmly's real differentiation is that it doesn't stop at identifying anonymous visitors — it pairs that data with two purpose-built agents that act on it: an Inbound Agent that engages whoever is already on the site, and a TAM Agent that maps and works accounts that aren't there yet, both drawing on the same combined first/second/third-party signal layer. Real named customers (New Relic, Cyberhaven, CircleCI) and $21.9M raised since 2020 back a company past the earliest stage. The honest catches: person-level identification (the harder, more valuable half of "de-anonymization") is independently reported well below what specialist identification tools claim, and as of today there is no self-serve monthly plan or free tier at all — every paid tier is a quarterly-or-annual contract starting at $4,875/quarter. Pick Warmly if you have real inbound volume and want one system for both engaging visitors and orchestrating outbound around them; skip it if you want to trial something free or month-to-month first, or if your traffic doesn't clear the volume where person-level matching pays off.

listings.name: Warp
listings.tagline: The AI-native terminal that replaces your shell and orchestrates Claude Code, Codex and its own Warp Agent side by side.
listings.verdict: Warp is the one listing in this category that isn't really competing with Claude Code or Codex CLI so much as hosting them: it's a full terminal replacement whose headline capability is running multiple vendors' coding agents side by side in one place, with team-wide context (Warp Drive), a real API for triggering cloud agent runs programmatically (Oz), and — since April 2026 — a genuinely open-source client backed by 63.6k GitHub stars and OpenAI as founding sponsor. The tradeoff is scope: adopting Warp means switching your terminal application, not just adding a CLI tool, and its paid tiers are metered in credits that can climb fast under heavy daily use — the $200/month Max tier exists precisely because Build's 1,500 credits run out for power users. Pick Warp if you want one AI-native home for every coding agent you use and are willing to make it your default terminal; stick with a standalone CLI agent if you'd rather keep your current terminal untouched.

listings.name: Webhound
listings.tagline: An AI research agent priced by the dollar, not a subscription — set a budget, get a cited report or a sourced dataset back, with a native MCP server for Claude, Codex and Cursor.
listings.verdict: Webhound's pitch is refreshingly literal: give it a research task and a dollar figure, and it keeps searching, reading and verifying until the budget runs out, with no subscription, no seat count and none of the opaque per-action credit pricing some rival agents use. Its two output modes are a real point of difference inside this site's research-agents category: a Report reads like a cited answer, while a Dataset behaves more like a structured deliverable, but with a source trail attached to every individual value rather than just the document as a whole, genuinely useful for market-mapping or lead-list work and not only narrative Q&A. Its MCP server is the other real differentiator: Claude, Codex and Cursor can trigger a Webhound run and read the output as a tool call, an integration none of this category's other listings currently offer as a first-class feature. The honest catches: this is a two-person, YC-backed team that has already rebuilt its own pricing and interface more than once since a mid-2025 launch as a free tool, its own blog is candid that building trust in AI-generated research is still an open problem it is actively working on rather than a solved one, and it makes no claim to a specialized corpus the way Elicit, Undermind or GC AI do — it researches the open web generally, same as Perplexity or GPT Researcher, just priced and delivered differently. Pick Webhound for agent-triggered research callable from inside Claude Code or Cursor, or for a sourced dataset rather than a narrative report; look elsewhere if a specialized corpus or an established, multi-year track record matters more than novel pricing and delivery.

listings.name: Windsurf (now Devin Desktop)
listings.tagline: The agentic IDE that was Codeium, then Windsurf, now Cognition’s Devin Desktop, a command centre for coding agents.
listings.verdict: Windsurf was one of the best agentic IDEs of its generation, and as Devin Desktop it is now something more ambitious: a vendor-neutral command centre where local and cloud agents — Cognition’s own plus Claude Agent and Codex via the open ACP — run inside one polished editor (Gemini CLI could too, but Google restricted free access to it in June 2026, and its Antigravity CLI replacement isn’t ACP-compatible yet). That openness is a real differentiator in a field of walled-garden tools, and the shared free/$20 subscription with Devin makes it easy to try. The cost is turbulence: Codeium became Windsurf, Windsurf became Devin Desktop, and the original Cascade agent was switched off on 1 July 2026 — a lot of change for a tool teams use daily. Its default SWE models are also a notch behind frontier models on the hardest tasks, though you can route to those. Pick it if you want an open, multi-agent desktop IDE and are comfortable inside Cognition’s ecosystem; skip it if you want a lightweight editor extension or you specifically wanted the standalone Windsurf that no longer exists.

listings.name: Zed
listings.tagline: The open-source, GPU-native code editor built from scratch by Atom's creators — runs Claude Code, Codex and other agents via the open Agent Client Protocol it created. Free forever; Pro from $10/month.
listings.verdict: Zed's real differentiation in this index isn't a single proprietary agent, it's the platform decision underneath every rival: Cursor and Windsurf both forked VS Code and built one closed-source agent into it; GitHub Copilot is tied to GitHub's own stack. Zed rebuilt the editor from zero in Rust for GPU-native performance, then open-sourced the connection layer itself — the Agent Client Protocol — so Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot and others run natively inside Zed as swappable External Agents, and JetBrains now speaks the same protocol in its own IDEs. That buys real vendor-independence and raw editor speed, but it's genuinely earlier-stage on ecosystem maturity: Zed's own extension catalog is, in its own words, "hundreds" of community packages against VS Code's much larger marketplace; remote development requires bringing your own SSH-reachable server (no managed, Codespaces-style cloud environment, and Windows isn't yet supported as a remote target); and its DAP-based debugger — documented as breakpoints, stepping and variable inspection — doesn't list the watch-window and data-breakpoint features VS Code's debugger has had for years. Pick Zed if editor performance and not being locked into one vendor's built-in agent matter more to you than ecosystem breadth; stay on Cursor or GitHub Copilot for the single most mature, batteries-included agent experience today.

listings.name: Zendesk AI Agents
listings.tagline: The AI agent built into Zendesk's own helpdesk Suite — resolves tickets across messaging, email and voice, billed per Verified Resolution on top of a per-seat plan.
listings.verdict: Zendesk AI Agents' real pitch isn't that it out-resolves Fin or Decagon — it's that the agent ships inside the helpdesk platform millions of support teams already run tickets on, so there's no second vendor, no separate integration project, and a multi-model backbone (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Bedrock) that isn't locked to one provider. The May 2026 billing restructuring is a genuine improvement: it stopped charging for escalations and abandoned conversations, addressing exactly the "assumed resolution" complaint that dogs Intercom Fin. But convenience costs predictability: AI Agents aren't sold standalone, so total spend stacks a $55-$115+/agent/month Suite fee on top of an undisclosed per-resolution rate that independent analysis puts around $1.20-$1.50 — and that rate has already been restructured once in 2026, so multi-year cost modeling means trusting a moving target rather than a stable, published price like Fin's $0.99/resolution. Pick Zendesk AI Agents if you're already on (or moving to) Zendesk and want one vendor for tickets and AI; pick Fin or a standalone specialist instead if you want the AI agent decoupled from your helpdesk choice, or a single number you can budget against.

listings.name: Zot
listings.tagline: A free, MIT-licensed coding-agent harness in one Go binary, branch any session from any past message and view it as a tree, plus a Telegram bridge.
listings.verdict: Zot earns its place with a real, working idea: fork any past message in a coding session into a new branch and see the whole tree at a glance, all from one free, MIT-licensed Go binary with no Docker or Node runtime. It backs that up with genuine breadth — 30+ model providers, local Ollama support, a Telegram bridge, background swarm subagents, and an importable Go SDK for developers who want to build their own harness on top of it — and it ships fast, with 303 releases and 10+ contributors since an April 2026 start. The honest catches are the ones the maintainer discloses directly: the OAuth-reuse trick that lets it bill through a Claude/ChatGPT subscription is, by the README's own admission, a likely terms-of-service violation that could be revoked at any time (the API-key flow sidesteps this), the docs call the project "beta forever" rather than production-stable, and the TUI is admitted to be almost entirely AI-generated. Pick Zot if you want a free, fast, Go-native harness with real branching-session control and are comfortable with fast-moving independent software; pick Juggler instead if you want the same branching-tree idea with a GUI, or a first-party vendor tool if you need managed support and want to avoid any OAuth-reuse risk entirely.
